Sweet Woodruff (and some other plants I haven't yet killed)

Hello again folks! It's the end of May and I've been quiet for a while, so here's an update for y'all from US Hardiness Zone 4.

  • Identify your wildflowers! Some of them are really cool.

We poked through all the plants in an old overgrown porch and decided what to keep - irises, some thyme, lamb's ears and a mysterious plant I couldn't identify. Wildflower books were no help, it was only once we showed a greenhouse owner pictures of the plant that they recognized it as Sweet Woodruff. It's not just pretty, it's an edible and fragrant ground cover that grows like crazy!

  • If you till your ground, pull up the sod first. Grass re-grows really quick.

Last fall I tilled a garden plot for myself but I was too lazy to pull out the grass first. Big mistake! A heavy tiller went through it fine, but when I came back in the spring I found a plot full of healthy sod roots that were impossible to spade through and already growing leaves.

I carefully scalped up all the sod and re-tilled with a tiny little electric machine over Memorial weekend. Those things may weigh only a few pounds, but they have plenty of power! It looked nice and clean.

  • There are some clever containers you can use for plants, but be careful.

I found these on discount at the garden store for $2.50 a container. They're just a big huge block of the same coconut coir stuff those little expanding pucks are made from. They were cheap and they drain nicely, but I have to be careful to keep them from getting too hot in the direct sun. As I learned last summer with container planting, just because leaves can handle the heat of direct sunlight doesn't mean that roots can as well!

  • Finally, some garden photos!

Blue are tomatoes, purple are peppers, and the two green marks are the tips of horseradish roots as they recover from transplanting. I'm particularly happy with the horseradish. Next up I'll be filling the rest of the tilled space with onions, beans, peas, radishes and carrots. I put some squash and watermelon inside of a few old tires, hoping that they'll sprawl out well enough to help control the grass. As you can see there's quite a bit of grass out there, and I really don't like the idea of hacking it back every few days! Some landscaping fabric and mulch will help as well.
